# Getting started

This notebook pairs the R examples with Python code and output.
The language tabs are synchronized throughout the document.
Both languages use the saved data in the accompanying `data` folder.
The original download examples remain available but are not run during rendering.
Fitting routines and random initialization can produce different results between languages.

## Required packages

Quarto uses knitr and reticulate; install reticulate 1.41 or later.
The loading chunk declares the Python dependencies for reticulate's managed environment.
The neural network examples use Keras 2.15 and TensorFlow 2.15, matching the R `keras` interface.
For an existing Python environment, install `numpy<2`, pandas, scipy, matplotlib, seaborn, statsmodels, requests, yfinance, plotly, arch, `keras==2.15.*`, and `tensorflow==2.15.*`.
Select that environment with `RETICULATE_PYTHON` before rendering if needed.
Render with `quarto render 4_advanced_models_R_Python.qmd`.
Training the networks takes longer than the statistical examples.


::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## Fetching some (crypto) data

The download snippets show CoinMarketCap through R's `crypto2` and Yahoo Finance through Python's `yfinance`.
They are optional; the calculations below use the same saved prices in both languages.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-02-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| eval: false

coins <- crypto_list() 
c_info <- crypto_info(coin_list = coins, limit = 30)
coin_names <- c("Bitcoin", "Ethereum", "Tether USDt", "BNB", "USDC", "Solana")
coin_hist <- crypto_history(coins |> dplyr::filter(name %in% coin_names),
                            start_date = "20170101",
                            end_date = "20251206")
coin_hist <- coin_hist |>  # Timestamps are at midnight, hence we add a day.
  dplyr::mutate(date = 1 + as.Date(as.POSIXct(timestamp, origin="1970-01-01")))
coin_hist <- coin_hist |> 
  group_by(name) |>
  mutate(return = close / lag(close) - 1 ) |>
  ungroup()
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

````{python}
#| label: example-02-python
#| warning: false
#| eval: false

coin_tickers = {"BTC-USD": ("bitcoin", "Bitcoin", "BTC"),
                "ETH-USD": ("ethereum", "Ethereum", "ETH"),
                "USDT-USD": ("tether", "Tether USDt", "USDT"),
                "BNB-USD": ("bnb", "BNB", "BNB"),
                "USDC-USD": ("usd-coin", "USDC", "USDC"),
                "SOL-USD": ("solana", "Solana", "SOL")}
quotes = yf.download(list(coin_tickers), start="2017-01-01", end="2025-12-07",
                     auto_adjust=False, progress=False)
closes = quotes["Close"].reindex(columns=list(coin_tickers))
closes.index.name = "date"
coin_hist = (closes.reset_index().melt(id_vars="date", var_name="ticker", value_name="close")
             .dropna(subset=["close"]))
for column, position in [("slug", 0), ("name", 1), ("symbol", 2)]:
    coin_hist[column] = coin_hist["ticker"].map(lambda ticker: coin_tickers[ticker][position])
coin_hist = coin_hist.sort_values(["name", "date"])
coin_hist["return"] = coin_hist.groupby("name")["close"].pct_change(fill_method=None)
````

# ARCH-type models


## Realized volatility

Then, let's have a look at volatility. It's measured as

$$v_t=\sqrt{\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{s=0}^{T-1}(r_{t-s}-\bar{r}_t)^2},$$
where $\bar{r}_t$ is the mean return in the window of $T$ observations. 
Below, we compute the rolling standard deviation over 20 days.
Each window ends on the date shown.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-03-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false

coin_hist <- coin_hist |>
  arrange(name, date) |>
  group_by(name) |>
  filter(!is.na(return)) |>
  mutate(real_vol_20 = RcppRoll::roll_sd(return, n = 20, fill = NA, align = "right")) |>
  ungroup()
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

````{python}
#| label: example-03-python
#| warning: false

coin_hist = coin_hist.dropna(subset=["return"]).sort_values(["name", "date"]).copy()
coin_hist["real_vol_20"] = coin_hist.groupby("name")["return"].transform(
    lambda values: values.rolling(20).std(ddof=1))
````

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}

#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

coin_hist |>
  filter(name == "Bitcoin") |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(c("close", "real_vol_20")), names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = series)) + geom_line() + theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(vars(series), nrow = 2, scales = "free")# + scale_y_log10()
```

Now let's have a look a the autocorrelation of the volatility: it's highly persistent.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-05-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4

crypto_acf <- coin_hist |> 
  na.omit() %>%
  split(.$name) %>% 
  map(~acf(.$real_vol_20, plot = F)) %>% 
  map_dfr(
    ~data.frame(lag = .$lag, 
                acf = .$acf,
                ci = qnorm(0.975)/sqrt(.$n.used)
    ), .id = "name") 
crypto_acf |> 
  filter(lag > 0, lag < 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lag, y = acf, fill = name)) + 
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.8) + theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", end = 0.9, begin = 0.1)
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

````{python}
#| label: example-05-python
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4

crypto_acf = []
for name, group in coin_hist.groupby("name"):
    values = group["real_vol_20"].dropna().to_numpy()
    coefficients = acf(values, nlags=14, fft=True)
    crypto_acf.extend({"name": name, "lag": lag, "acf": coefficients[lag]}
                      for lag in range(1, 15))
crypto_acf = pd.DataFrame(crypto_acf)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
sns.barplot(data=crypto_acf, x="lag", y="acf", hue="name", palette="magma", ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Lag", ylabel="Autocorrelation")
ax.legend(title="Coin", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
````

:::


Large price movements often occur close together.
GARCH models allow the variance of returns to change through time. 


The realized volatility is based on **past** returns. But markets (**equity** mostly) have another very cool and forward-looking indicator called the [**VIX**](https://www.cboe.com/tradable_products/vix/). The VIX is slightly different, because it is based on forward-looking option prices (taking their implied volatilities over specific horizons). Still, it is linked (empirically) to the traditional volatility. 

Let's have a look below.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

```{r}
VIX <- VIX |> as.data.frame() |>
```

Periods of high volatility tend to occur together, forming **volatility clusters**. 

## Some theory

Therefore, we also need to introduce models that allow for this type of feature. In 1982, Robert Engle proposed such a model, called [**ARCH**](https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912773) for "*AutoRegressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity*", 
which was generalized in 1986 to [**GARCH**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0304407686900631) models. Engle obtained the Nobel Prize in economics in part for this contribution. 

As we show below, GARCH models have a direct link with auto-regressive processes! 

The idea is to work with the innovations, $e_t$ and to specify them a bit differently, i.e., like this: $e_t=\sigma_t z_t$, where $\sigma_t$ is going to be a changing standard deviation and $z_t$ is a simple white noise. What matters is that the vol term is modelled as
$$\sigma^2_t = a+\sum_{j=1}^pd_j\sigma^2_{t-j} + \sum_{k=1}^qb_ke^2_{t-k},$$
hence, the value of $\sigma_t^2$ depends both on its past and on the past of squared innovations. 

There have been MANY extension to these models: T-GARCH, E-GARCH, etc. See for instance [GARCH models: structure, statistical inference and financial applications](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9781119313472). 

## Examples: estimation

There are many packages for GARCH estimation. We propose two: [**ruGARCH**](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rugarch/index.html) and [**fGARCH**](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/fGarch/index.html).


In **fGARCH**, the model is: 

$$\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha e_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2.$$ 
In the output, there are some additional parameters that allow to propose a more general model:

- **shape** is the shape parameter of the conditional distribution.   
- **skew** is the skewness parameter of the conditional distribution.   
- **delta** a numeric value, the exponent delta of the variance recursion, fixed at 2 usually. 

$\delta$ values other than 2 come from P-GARCH models:

\begin{align}
\varepsilon_t & = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \text{Skew}(\text{shape},\text{skew}), \\ 
\sigma_t^{\delta}
&= \omega
  + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i\bigl(|\varepsilon_{t-i}| - \gamma_i \varepsilon_{t-i}\bigr)^{\delta}
  + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j\,\sigma_{t-j}^{\delta},
\end{align}

The examples below use Gaussian innovations and a constant mean.
Other distribution choices allow for skewness or heavier tails.
Returns are expressed in percentage points for these fits.
Python uses the [arch package](https://arch.readthedocs.io/en/latest/univariate/introduction.html), first through its model constructor, then through separate components. 

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-07-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false

btc_returns <- coin_hist |> filter(name == "Bitcoin") |> pull(return) |> na.omit()
garch_returns <- 100 * btc_returns
fit_f <- garchFit(formula = ~garch(1, 1), data = garch_returns,
                   cond.dist = "norm", trace = FALSE)
fit_f
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

````{python}
#| label: example-07-python
#| warning: false

btc_returns = coin_hist.loc[coin_hist["name"].eq("Bitcoin"), "return"].dropna()
garch_returns = 100 * btc_returns
fit_f = arch_model(garch_returns, mean="Constant", vol="GARCH", p=1, q=1,
                    dist="normal", rescale=False).fit(disp="off", cov_type="classic")
print(fit_f.summary())
````

:::

Now, with **rugarch**...

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-08-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false

spec <- ugarchspec(variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
                   mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
                   distribution.model = "norm")
garch_dates <- coin_hist |> filter(name == "Bitcoin") |> pull(date)
garch_series <- xts::xts(garch_returns, order.by = garch_dates)
fit_r <- ugarchfit(data = garch_series, spec = spec, solver = "hybrid")
fit_r@fit$coef
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

````{python}
#| label: example-08-python
#| warning: false

garch_components = ConstantMean(garch_returns, volatility=GARCH(p=1, q=1),
                                 distribution=Normal(), rescale=False)
fit_r = garch_components.fit(disp="off", cov_type="classic")
print(fit_r.params)
````

:::


The packages use different fitting routines, so their estimates can differ.
In both R examples, the variance equation is
$$\sigma_t^2=\omega+\alpha e_{t-1}^2+\beta\sigma_{t-1}^2.$$
The coefficient $\alpha$ multiplies the squared shock; $\beta$ multiplies the previous variance. 

With both libraries, it is possible to make predictions.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-09-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false

predict(fit_f, n.ahead = 5)
ugarchforecast(fit_r, n.ahead = 3)
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

````{python}
#| label: example-09-python
#| warning: false

forecast_f = fit_f.forecast(horizon=5, reindex=False)
forecast_r = fit_r.forecast(horizon=3, reindex=False)
print(pd.DataFrame({"horizon": np.arange(1, 6),
                    "mean": forecast_f.mean.iloc[-1].to_numpy(),
                    "standard_deviation": np.sqrt(forecast_f.variance.iloc[-1].to_numpy())})
      .to_string(index=False))
print(pd.DataFrame({"horizon": np.arange(1, 4),
                    "mean": forecast_r.mean.iloc[-1].to_numpy(),
                    "standard_deviation": np.sqrt(forecast_r.variance.iloc[-1].to_numpy())})
      .to_string(index=False))
````

:::

The reported standard deviations are daily volatilities in percentage points.    

A cool feature of `{rugarch}` is that you can use forward rolling, as in actual **backtests** (more on that below). 






# Vector Auto-Regression

## The VAR(1) model

Now we are switching to full multivariate mode!    
With the **Vector Auto-Regression** (VAR). It is written as:

$$X_t = \mu + A X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t,
\qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{i.i.d. } (0,\Sigma_\varepsilon),$$
with $X_t \in \mathbb{R}^k, \mu \in \mathbb{R}^k, A \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
##  Interpretation 
In two dimensions: $X_t=[X_{t,1} \ X_{t,2}  ]'$.      

$$X_t = \mu +  \begin{bmatrix} A_{11} & A_{12} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} \end{bmatrix} X_{t-1} + \text{error}$$

So $A_{11}$ measures the impact from $X_{t-1, 1}$ onto $X_{t,1}$ (itself) and same for $A_{22}$ for the second component. 
The non-diagonal terms drive the cross-effects: $A_{12}$ is the impact of $X_{t-1,2}$ on $X_{t,1}$ and vice-versa.  
:::

A few probabilistic properties. 

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Mean
If the VAR(1) is stable (all eigenvalues of $A$ satisfy $|\lambda_i(A)|<1$), the **unconditional mean** exists and is given by
$$\mathbb{E}[X_t] = (I - A)^{-1}\mu.$$
:::

Next, let $\Gamma_0 = \mathbb{V}(X_t)$, it must satisfy
$$ \Gamma_0 = A \Gamma_0 A' + \Sigma_\varepsilon.$$


Next, define the lag-$h$ autocovariance matrix:
$$\Gamma_h = \text{Cov}(X_t, X_{t-h}).$$

Using for simplicity $X_t = A X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ (the constant terms do not affect the covariances):
$$ \Gamma_h = \text{Cov}(A X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, X_{t-h}) = A \text{Cov}(X_{t-1}, X_{t-h}) + \underbrace{\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_t, X_{t-h})}_{=0}
= A \Gamma_{h-1} $$


::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Autocovariance

By recursion, we obtain the multivariate version of the AR(1):
$$\Gamma_h = A^h \Gamma_0, \quad h \ge 0.$$
The correlation matrix at lag $h$ is $D^{-1/2}\Gamma_h D^{-1/2}$, where $D$ contains the variances on its diagonal.
:::



## The VAR(p) Model

A Vector Autoregression of order $p$, denoted VAR($p$), models a $k$-dimensional time series vector 
$\mathbf{X}_t = (X_{1,t}, \dots, X_{k,t})^\top$ as:

$$
\mathbf{X}_t 
= \mathbf{c} + A_1 \mathbf{X}_{t-1} + A_2 \mathbf{X}_{t-2} + \cdots + A_p \mathbf{X}_{t-p} + \mathbf{e}_t,
$$

where:

- $\mathbf{X}_t$ is a $k \times 1$ vector of endogenous variables,   
- $\mathbf{c}$ is a $k \times 1$ vector of intercept terms,    
- $A_i$ are $k \times k$ coefficient matrices,     
- $\mathbf{e}_t$ is a $k \times 1$ vector of innovations (reduced-form errors).


**Error term assumptions**: the innovations satisfy

$$\mathbf{e}_t \sim (0, \Sigma_e),$$

where $\Sigma_e$ is a symmetric positive definite $k \times k$ covariance matrix, allowing contemporaneous correlation across equations.


## Empirics

VARs are often used on **macroeconomic** data.
The optional download code below uses the [World Bank API](https://data.worldbank.org/).  

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-10-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| eval: false

wb_raw <- WDI(                              # World Bank data
  indicator = c(
    "labor" = "SL.TLF.TOTL.IN",             # Labor force (# individuals)
    "savings_rate" = "NY.GDS.TOTL.ZS",      # Savings rate (% GDP)
    "inflation" = "FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG",         # Inflation rate
    "trade" = "NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS",             # Trade as % of GDP 
    "pop" = "SP.POP.TOTL",                  # Population
    "pop_growth" = "SP.POP.GROW",           # Population growth
    "capital_formation" = "NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS", # Gross capital formation (% GDP)
    "gdp_percap" = "NY.GDP.PCAP.CD",        # GDP per capita
    "RD_percap" = "GB.XPD.RSDV.GD.ZS",      # R&D per capita
    "educ_level" = "SE.SEC.CUAT.LO.ZS",     # % pop reachiing second. educ. level
    "educ_spending" = "SE.XPD.TOTL.GD.ZS",  # Education spending (%GDP)
    "nb_researchers" = "SP.POP.SCIE.RD.P6", # Nb researchers per million inhab.
    "debt" = "GC.DOD.TOTL.GD.ZS",           # Central gov. debt (% of GDP)
    "gdp" = "NY.GDP.MKTP.CD"                # Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
  ), 
  extra = TRUE,
  start = 1960,
  end = 2024) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.vector)) |>
  select(-status, -lending, -iso2c, -iso3c) |>  
  filter(region != "Aggregates", income != "Aggregates") |>
  arrange(country, year) |>
  group_by(country) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), impute)) |>
  mutate(gdp_growth = gdp_percap/dplyr::lag(gdp_percap) - 1, .before = "region") |>   
  ungroup() |>
  filter(lastupdated == max(lastupdated)) |>
  arrange(country, year)
```

````{python}
indicators = {"labor": "SL.TLF.TOTL.IN", "savings_rate": "NY.GDS.TOTL.ZS",
              "inflation": "FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG", "trade": "NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS",
              "pop": "SP.POP.TOTL", "pop_growth": "SP.POP.GROW",
              "capital_formation": "NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS", "gdp_percap": "NY.GDP.PCAP.CD",
              "RD_percap": "GB.XPD.RSDV.GD.ZS", "educ_level": "SE.SEC.CUAT.LO.ZS",
              "educ_spending": "SE.XPD.TOTL.GD.ZS", "nb_researchers": "SP.POP.SCIE.RD.P6",
              "debt": "GC.DOD.TOTL.GD.ZS", "gdp": "NY.GDP.MKTP.CD"}
wb_raw = pd.DataFrame({"year": np.arange(1960, 2025)})
for name, indicator in indicators.items():
    response = requests.get(f"https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/USA/indicator/{indicator}",
                            params={"format": "json", "date": "1960:2024", "per_page": 100},
                            timeout=120)
    response.raise_for_status()
    observations = response.json()[1]
    values = pd.DataFrame({"year": int(row["date"]), name: row["value"]}
                           for row in observations)
    wb_raw = wb_raw.merge(values, on="year", how="left")
wb_raw = wb_raw.sort_values("year")
wb_raw[list(indicators)] = wb_raw[list(indicators)].ffill(limit=6)
wb_raw["country"] = "United States"
wb_raw["gdp_growth"] = wb_raw["gdp_percap"].pct_change(fill_method=None)
````

# A primer on prediction

## Training/testing & co

The key idea is **backtest**: you have to put yourself in the shoes of someone living in the past. By this we mean, without knowledge of the future. To do this, you need to consider a loop that spans different dates in the past. At each point in time $t$ you:

1. extract the data available at time $t$;   
2. build a predictive model;   
3. make some prediction based on the currently available data;    
4. evaluate the accuracy of the prediction thanks to the (future) realized values.   

A simplified diagram below.   

![](images/backtest.png){width=600}


## Some code

Even though it's ugly, we will resort to loops.   
Below, we focus on the simple case of a unique series (bitcoin) and a simple model (ARMA), but this can be applied to much more complex situations and models.   
In the code below, we

1. build predictions;     
2. derive the corresponding errors;    
3. implement a trading strategy (we buy if returns are predicted to be positive and short sell otheriwse). 

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-13-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false

btc <- coin_hist |>
  filter(name == "Bitcoin", lubridate::wday(date) == 2) |>
  select(date, close) |> arrange(date) |>
  mutate(end_date = lead(date), fwd_return = lead(close) / close - 1) |> drop_na()
buffer <- 100
tc <- 0.001
trading_dates <- btc$date[(buffer + 1):nrow(btc)]
period_end_dates <- btc$end_date[(buffer + 1):nrow(btc)]
pred <- err <- strat_ret <- numeric(length(trading_dates))
previous_position <- 0
for (j in seq_along(trading_dates)) {
  train <- btc |> filter(date < trading_dates[j])
  fit <- arima(train$fwd_return, order = c(1, 0, 1), include.mean = TRUE)
  pred[j] <- as.numeric(predict(fit, n.ahead = 1)$pred[1])
  realized <- btc |> filter(date == trading_dates[j]) |> pull(fwd_return)
  err[j] <- realized - pred[j]
  position <- sign(pred[j])
  strat_ret[j] <- realized * position - tc * abs(position - previous_position)
  previous_position <- position
}
strat_ret[length(strat_ret)] <- tail(strat_ret, 1) - tc * abs(previous_position)
c(forecast_weeks = length(pred))
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

````{python}
#| label: example-13-python
#| warning: false

btc = (coin_hist.loc[coin_hist["name"].eq("Bitcoin") & coin_hist["date"].dt.weekday.eq(0),
                     ["date", "close"]].sort_values("date").copy())
btc["end_date"] = btc["date"].shift(-1)
btc["fwd_return"] = btc["close"].shift(-1) / btc["close"] - 1
btc = btc.dropna().reset_index(drop=True)
buffer = 100
tc = 0.001
trading_dates = btc["date"].iloc[buffer:].reset_index(drop=True)
period_end_dates = btc["end_date"].iloc[buffer:].reset_index(drop=True)
pred = np.empty(len(trading_dates))
err = np.empty(len(trading_dates))
strat_ret = np.empty(len(trading_dates))
previous_position = 0
for j, current_date in enumerate(trading_dates):
    train = btc.loc[btc["date"] < current_date, "fwd_return"].to_numpy()
    fit = ARIMA(train, order=(1, 0, 1), trend="c").fit()
    pred[j] = fit.forecast(steps=1)[0]
    realized = btc.loc[btc["date"].eq(current_date), "fwd_return"].iloc[0]
    err[j] = realized - pred[j]
    position = np.sign(pred[j])
    strat_ret[j] = realized * position - tc * abs(position - previous_position)
    previous_position = position
strat_ret[-1] -= tc * abs(previous_position)
print("Forecast weeks:", len(pred))
````

## What really matters (in finance)

Models (and people) often focus on loss (objective) functions.    
In finance, we usually try to forecast returns, hence the loss function is the (root-) **Mean Squared Error**:

$$\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T (r_t-\tilde{r}_t)^2, $$

where $r_t$ is the realized return and $\tilde{r}_t$ is the model return. Assuming predictions are unbiased $(\mathbb{E}[r_t]=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{r}_t])$, then (after some math...)

$$\text{MSE} = \mathbb{E}[(r_t - \tilde{r}_t)^2]=\mathbb{V}[r_t]+\mathbb{V}[\tilde{r}_t]-2\text{Cov}(r_t, \tilde{r}_t)$$

**Question**: which of these terms matter the most?    

- the **variance of realized returns**: nothing we can do about that.    
- the **variance of predicted returns**: this enters the variace-bias tradeoff; but it's not super clear what the impact it can have.   
- the **correlation between predicted and realized returns**: this is the CRUX!!! This measures the accuracy (very similar to the hit ratio!)




# Advanced temporal models

Before we can move towards chronology-based neural networks, we must explain how simple, feed-forward, NNs work.

## (Feedforward) neural networks

A few images help explain how simple NNs work.

First, the **structure**. The network takes an input which is then processed via many multiplications, additions and activations.   
At the very end, we get the output. It can be a simple number, but could also be more complex (vector, matrix, etc.).  

![](images/NN_scheme.png){width=800 fig-align="center"}

The intermediate **activation** functions are there to break the linearity. A few examples below: 

![](images/activation.png){width=500 fig-align="center"}


Next, the **training**. This phase is intended to determine "good" parameter values. Obviously, the "best" parameters would be ideal, but they are out of reach (the problem is too complex). 

The core idea is **gradient descent**: we seek to minimize a loss function (e.g., the MSE) and this depends on the derivative:

![](images/Newton.png){width=600 fig-align="center"}

Now, there is a very interesting process called **backpropagation** that involves lots of computations of derivatives (skipped here):

![](images/backprop.png){width=800 fig-align="center"}

Training searches for weights that reduce the loss; it need not reach a local minimum.  
But they depend on the **training sample**: whether they work well out-of-sample (on testing sets) is another question.   
If yes, the model is said to **generalize** well. 
That's the great quest of machine learning.  


::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
An important property of NNs is that they are **universal approximators**: Any continuous function $f$ can be **approximated up to arbitrary precision** (on a finite interval) by a single layer perceptron with smooth (bounded continuous) activation function.   
This is an approximation result; it does not guarantee that training will find suitable weights. 
:::



## Recurrent networks


Feed-forward have zero memory. How can we bring some in the model?   

![](images/RNN.png){width=600}

Problem: **vanishing gradients**...
Hence: longer term memory! **LSTM** or **GRU**...


::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Gated recurrent units
The system of equations is the following
\begin{align*}
\tilde{y}_i&=z_i\tilde{y}_{i-1}+ (1-z_i)\tanh \left(\textbf{w}_y'\textbf{x}_i+ b_y+ u_yr_i\tilde{y}_{i-1}\right) \quad \textcolor{red}{\text{output}} \\
z_i &= \text{sig}(\textbf{w}_z'\textbf{x}_i+b_z+u_z\tilde{y}_{i-1})  \quad \textcolor{red}{\text{`update gate'}} \ \in (0,1)\\
r_i &= \text{sig}(\textbf{w}_r'\textbf{x}_i+b_r+u_r\tilde{y}_{i-1}) \quad \textcolor{red}{\text{`reset gate'}}  \ \in (0,1)
\end{align*}
:::


Preparing the data should follow this principle/structure

Sequence 1: [price_day1, price_day2, ..., price_day10] → target: price_day11   
Sequence 2: [price_day2, price_day3, ..., price_day11] → target: price_day12   
Sequence 3: [price_day3, price_day4, ..., price_day12] → target: price_day13

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-18-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false

n <- length(nvda)
look_back <- 20
X <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n - look_back, ncol = look_back)
y <- numeric(n - look_back)
for (i in seq_len(n - look_back)) {
  X[i, ] <- nvda[i:(i + look_back - 1)]
  y[i] <- nvda[i + look_back]
}
target_dates <- nvda_dates[(look_back + 1):n]
train_size <- floor(0.8 * nrow(X))
head(X[, 1:5])
```

## Code for universal approximation

A first model.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-25-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false

tensorflow::set_random_seed(42, disable_gpu = FALSE)

model_ua <- keras_model_sequential()
model_ua %>%   # This defines the structure of the network, i.e. how layers are organized
  layer_dense(units = 16, activation = 'sigmoid', input_shape = 1) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1) # 
model_ua %>% keras::compile(                      # Model specification
  loss = 'mean_squared_error',                  # Loss function
  optimizer = optimizer_rmsprop(),              # Optimisation method (weight updating)
  metrics = c('mean_absolute_error')            # Output metric
)
summary(model_ua)   

fit_ua <- model_ua %>% 
  fit(seq(0, 6, by = 0.001) %>% matrix(ncol = 1),              # Training data = x
      sin(seq(0, 6, by = 0.001)) %>% matrix(ncol = 1),         # Training label = y
      verbose = 0,
      epochs = 30, batch_size = 64                             # Training parameters
  )
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

````{python}
#| label: example-25-python
#| warning: false

keras.utils.set_random_seed(42)
model_ua = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Input(shape=(1,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(16, activation="sigmoid"),
    keras.layers.Dense(1)])
model_ua.compile(loss="mean_squared_error", optimizer=keras.optimizers.RMSprop(),
                 metrics=["mean_absolute_error"])
model_ua.summary()
ua_x = np.linspace(0, 6, 6001, dtype="float32").reshape(-1, 1)
fit_ua = model_ua.fit(ua_x, np.sin(ua_x), epochs=30, batch_size=64, verbose=0)
````

The comparisons.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

```{r}
#| label: example-27-r
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4

ua_grid <- seq(0, 6, by = 0.001)
tibble(x = ua_grid,
       `Small model` = as.numeric(predict(model_ua, matrix(ua_grid, ncol = 1), verbose = 0)),
       `Large model` = as.numeric(predict(model_ua2, matrix(ua_grid, ncol = 1), verbose = 0)),
       `sin(x)` = sin(ua_grid)) |>
  pivot_longer(-x, names_to = "model", values_to = "output") |>
  ggplot(aes(x, output, color = model)) + geom_line() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Large model" = "#3366CC", "Small model" = "#EEAA33",
                                "sin(x)" = "#000000")) + theme_bw()
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}

````{python}
#| label: example-27-python
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4

ua_grid = np.linspace(0, 6, 6001, dtype="float32").reshape(-1, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(ua_grid.ravel(), model_ua.predict(ua_grid, verbose=0).ravel(),
        label="Small model", color="#EEAA33")
ax.plot(ua_grid.ravel(), model_ua2.predict(ua_grid, verbose=0).ravel(),
        label="Large model", color="#3366CC")
ax.plot(ua_grid.ravel(), np.sin(ua_grid).ravel(), label="sin(x)", color="black")
ax.set(xlabel="x", ylabel="Output")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
````

:::
